content: Indoor GNSS is not merely imprecise, it is structurally unusable, and this is the strongest technical argument for not bolting GPS onto a QR checkpoint system. Measured figures: indoor A-GPS 2D RMS accuracy is about 4m/7m in small wooden or brick houses and up to 60m deep indoors in a tower block; non-assisted GPS is often unavailable deep indoors with time-to-first-fix over a minute; a three-storey commercial building walk test had position fixes available 97 percent of the time but more than half of the fixes placed the user outside the building. Mechanism: GNSS signals are attenuated 20-30 dB by office buildings and more than 30 dB underground (a plywood wall costs 2.3 dB; cinder block and concrete ten times more), and indoor multipath/NLOS dominates because the direct path is attenuated or eliminated while reflected and diffracted paths dominate - indoor signal levels are attenuated 25-35 dB versus 10-25 dB outdoors in a city, beyond what conventional algorithms can accommodate; the observed indoor pseudorange delay can reach 100m. The CTIA technical paper on indoor E911 accuracy lists the causes as severe multipath distortion, NLOS conditions, high attenuation and scattering, fast temporal change from people and opening doors, and temperature/pressure diversity across floors. The FCC's own indoor accuracy test bed found A-GPS met the 50m requirement in rural morphologies but not in dense urban or indoor environments, and did not test vertical accuracy at all. The QRAuth protocol-design page draws the practical conclusion for QR systems specifically: 'Indoor environments have no GPS signal at all and fall back to WiFi triangulation (+/-15-40m) or cell tower triangulation (+/-100-300m)', so a geo-radius check cannot distinguish two codes on opposite sides of a building. For this project the implication is that any claim of outdoor/GPS-assisted indoor positioning is a false claim, and that the honest system statement is that position is known exactly at scan instants and nowhere else.
